In the printed tradition, are the accents of the Decalogue grammatical?

The question

The two Decalogues are each chanted two ways: the טעם תחתון division into ordinary-length verses, and the טעם עליון division by commandment, which makes the short prohibitions (לא תרצח, לא תנאף, לא תגנב) their own tiny verses and folds long passages into single long ones. Issue #36 grammar-checked the Tiberian-manuscript (WLC / MAM) תחתון and עליון threads by detangling WLC’s dual cantillation. This page (issue #52) asks the companion question for the printed editions (דפוסים, also Koren and Simanim): fed through the very same prose grammar checker, are their תחתון and עליון accentuations grammatical too?

Unlike the manuscript thread, the printed and manuscript readings are already single cantillation, spelled out word-for-word on the Wikisource base page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים. Each chanted verse (delimited by its own sof pasuq) is fed through the shared pipeline — a leading verse-start token, the prose scanner, then the prose PLY grammar — exactly as issue #36 does. The manuscript versions are the baseline (MAM’s own authoritative text, expected all clean); the printed versions are the object of study.

The verdict

Tiberian manuscriptPrinted editions
Exodus 20 — taḥton (lower)✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Exodus 20 — elyon (upper)✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)
Deuteronomy 5 — taḥton (lower)✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Deuteronomy 5 — elyon (upper)✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)

תחתון is grammatical everywhere — both books, both traditions. The printed תחתון differs from the manuscript only in details that do not touch the accent grammar (vocalization such as תִּרְצַח vs תִּרְצָח at לא תרצח, and where a maqaf or ga‘ya falls), and in one verse boundary: the printed תחתון ends its first verse at מבית עבדים (so it has one more verse than the manuscript, which runs the first two commandments together). Both parse clean.

עליון is grammatical in the manuscript but not in the printed editions: the printed עליון of each Decalogue has exactly one ungrammatical chanted verse — its opening one.

The four strands of אנכי…עבדים

The manuscript and printed traditions accent the Decalogue's אנכי…עבדים unit differently. The accent on עבדים is what decides the structure: a silluq + sof pasuq there ends the verse, so אנכי…עבדים stands as its own verse; an etnaḥta or revia there is mid-verse, folding אנכי…עבדים into a longer verse. In the two folding strands the range below shows עבדים in the middle, so its structure-deciding accent is on view:

mTאנכי֙…עבד֑ים…על־פנֽי׃
mEאנכ֖י…עבדֽים׃
pT
pEאנכי֙…עבד֗ים…מצותֽי׃

How many chanted verses each strand divides the Exodus Decalogue into:

strandchanted verses (Exodus)
m-trad תחתון12
m-trad עליון10
p-trad תחתון13
p-trad עליון9
  • Printed תחתון = manuscript עליון. Once אנכי…עבדים is its own verse there is only one grammatical way to accent it — etnaḥta in the middle, silluq at the end — so both traditions land on the same marks (consonants, accents, and accent-boundary marks: sof pasuq, maqaf, legarmeh). They differ only by an immaterial meteg (which the stripped range cells above drop, so their shared cell is one rowspan).
  • Printed עליון ≠ manuscript עליון. The printed עליון puts revia on עבדים and runs the first two commandments together into one verse (→ 9 total), where the manuscript עליון closes on silluq (→ 10).
  • The manuscript תחתון does not give אנכי…עבדים its own verse either — it runs אנכי…פני together (etnaḥta at עבדים, sof pasuq at פני), a third structure again.

Only one of these four strands is ungrammatical — the printed עליון, whose merged opening verse the section below dissects.

Why the printed עליון fails: the merged first verse

In the manuscript עליון, the first commandment אָנֹכִי … עֲבָדִים is its own chanted verse, and לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים begins the next — two separate verses, both of which parse clean. The printed editions instead merge the first two commandments into a single verse (nine chanted verses in all, against the manuscript’s ten). That one merged verse is what the grammar rejects. Shown stripped to consonants and accents (MAM-simple style) and divided at the printed תחתון’s verse boundaries — one עליון verse (E) spanning the five ordinary תחתון verses (T) it merges:

Eאנכי֙…מצותֽי׃
Tאנכ֖י…עבדֽים׃לא־יהי֥ה…על־פנֽי׃לא־תעש֨ה…לאֽרץ׃לא־תשתחו֥ה…לשנאֽי׃וע֥שה…מצותֽי׃
e
t

The single etnaḥta falls at לְשֹׂנְאָי, leaving an over-long first half that carries a segolta plus three separate revia domains (at עֲבָדִים, עַל־פָּנַי, and לָאָרֶץ); the prose grammar cannot build it and returns a pashta_phrase error — the same failure, at the same structural point, in both Decalogues.

The cause is the merged structure, not sheer length: Deuteronomy’s printed עליון Sabbath verse runs 55 words and parses clean, while this merged verse (51 words) does not. Keeping the two commandments as the manuscript’s two separate verses (9 and 42 words) is exactly what lets them parse.

A handful of wiki templates are resolved to plain pointed text (legarmeh/paseq to a paseq mark, qere for ketiv-qere, paragraph and pisqa markers dropped); the chanted verses are split at sof pasuq.
